Euro Digital: Europe is preparing money that will work even without the internet

Euro digital has taken a new step forward in Brussels.

The idea is for any citizen to be able to pay with a digital version of the euro, issued by the European Central Bank (ECB), including without an internet connection.

Payments can be made with a phone, card, online, and offline - and rely less on Visa, Mastercard, and private banks.

### What is already raising questions:
- Limits will be set on how much digital euros can be stored.
- Many stores may be required to accept it.
- Banks fear that some of the money will be taken from their accounts.
- Millions of citizens are concerned about privacy of data.

The ECB promises that digital euro will not replace cash, and offline payments will have an increased level of confidentiality (similar to cash).

However, the discussion in Europe has long gone beyond just the technology.

This is a question of power: do we need public digital money or are we opening the door to too much control over how we pay?

📌 Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): Portable IDs for Web3

Main Points
⏺ DIDs are identifiers you control, not usernames owned by platforms
⏺ They can link to verifiable credentials like diplomas or KYC checks
⏺ This post explains how DIDs help build portable identity across apps

1️⃣ What Is a DID — a standardized identifier tied to keys you own, not to an email, phone number, or single company.
2️⃣ Verifiable Credentials — organizations can sign claims about you (for example, “passed KYC”, “finished course”) that you can present elsewhere.
3️⃣ User Control — you decide when and where to share proofs instead of giving every app full personal data.
4️⃣ Interoperability — multiple dApps, wallets, and even Web2 services can recognize the same DID as “you”.
5️⃣ Privacy Angle — combined with zero-knowledge proofs, DIDs can prove facts (age, residency, reputation) without revealing raw documents.

Final Thoughts

Decentralized identifiers turn identity from siloed accounts into something you own and reuse — a core building block for Web3 logins and reputation.

Occupation by Invitation

Israel's Lebanon deal isn't a peace treaty; it's a legal rebranding of occupation with a nice press release and a very shaky fuse.
On paper, the IDF stays on "almost all" the territory it seized until Hezbollah is disarmed and its infrastructure "destroyed across Lebanon." 

That's not a benchmark; it's a blank check. You can call it "by invitation of the sovereign Lebanese state," but it converts a de facto occupation into a de jure "presence with permission," signed under massive military pressure — and the fact that Hezbollah ministers sit in the cabinet that signed it doesn't make it cleaner. It just folds the Lebanese state's fragmentation into Israel's legal shield.

The claim that "no one can now demand Israel withdraw" is wishful thinking dressed as lawfare. Iran, Turkey, France, the UN, the Arab states will still call it occupation if the IDF stays for years. The paper doesn't neutralize politics; it just hands Jerusalem a talking point in Brussels and Washington: "We're not occupiers, we're guests." 

That's why the EU rushed to bless the deal as a "critical step away from escalation" while cutting a modest refugee check — it lets everyone pretend something changed without forcing Israel to leave.
This isn't recognition; it's coercion. 

Beirut signed because it has no military alternative and hopes the army's deployment limits the next round of destruction. But for much of the public — not just Hezbollah's base — it reads as an enemy army left on their land. 

That's not durable legitimacy; it's a recipe for another round of "resistance," under Hezbollah's brand or a successor's.
The "pilot" withdrawals are a test balloon, and the asymmetry is baked in: Israel alone decides when the pilot has "failed," while Lebanon's only leverage is to threaten the one thing no one wants — renewed fighting. 

Meanwhile Lebanon is asked to holster its few non-military tools, from ICC filings to Western lobbying, in exchange for fewer airstrikes.
The biggest hole is domestic Israeli politics. 

The deal assumes the same leadership that walked into a two-front war will now manage a disciplined, low-profile "presence by invitation" — no overreach, no mission creep, no future government deciding to "adjust the lines" in ways that blow up the framework. 

It assumes a rationality recent history doesn't support.
So from a narrow legal-bureaucratic angle, it's a win: more legitimacy, more time, almost no withdrawal. 

From any wider perspective it's a frozen conflict with a nicer wrapper — a state-sanctioned occupation that keeps generating grievances for everyone who thrives on "resistance." 

If that's "a great success," it's the kind you only call great because all the other options are worse.

🔔 Ripple targets $1B revenue run rate without counting XRP holdings 

❗️ According to posts shared by CoinMarketCap and crypto-focused accounts on X, Ripple expects to end 2026 with a $1 billion revenue run rate. The figure does not include XRP held on Ripple’s balance sheet. That detail matters because Ripple has long faced public debate over the link between its business and XRP. Garlinghouse’s target frames the company as a fintech infrastructure provider that aims to earn money from products, clients, and services, not from token holdings or sales.

🌐 The deal also supports Ripple USD, known as RLUSD. Ripple has promoted the stablecoin for enterprise settlement and collateral use. Recently, crypto news reported that Ripple is also adding RLUSD to new payment tools, including services tied to AI agents and machine payments on the XRP Ledger. Company materials point to custody, treasury management, and liquidity services as core offerings. These products target banks and firms that need faster settlement, account control, and access to digital assets through regulated processes, rather than retail trading.
